title: Superteams
coreMove: Preserve disagreement long enough for it to improve the collective estimate before the group settles — a reservation voiced before consensus is a forecasting asset; the same reservation voiced after costs more and helps less.
sourcePressure: Superteams are not defined by harmony but by structure that keeps disagreement alive. Groupthink can degrade even a smart group when disagreement becomes socially expensive. Psychologically safe pushback and aggregation of multiple views before convergence are the mechanism. More people do not automatically yield better forecasting — it depends entirely on whether dissent remains operationally available at the moment it could still change the estimate.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong lesson is 'encourage diverse opinions' as a team norm, or 'run team brainstorms.' The precise point is structural and temporal: disagreement must remain socially safe to voice at the exact moment it would actually change the forecast — before the group has implicitly converged — not as a retrospective debrief.

hook: opening with 'Two heads are better than one' — generic teamwork truism
opening with generic management advice about diversity or inclusion
counterintuition: 'The best team is not the most harmonious team' — accurate but needs the structural mechanism, not just the slogan
tryThisNow: any prompt about scheduling team brainstorms or check-ins — misses the temporal specificity
'Tell your team you value dissent' — the chapter argues structural safety, not declarations
examples: any example where diversity of opinion is encouraged as a culture statement without the specific beat of dissent changing a collective estimate

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: Groupthink takes different forms in high-stakes professional teams — the variety of openings should show that the conformity pressure is universal, not specific to boardrooms

exampleSpecs.domain: emergency room triage team where a junior nurse has a different read on a patient's presentation than the attending physician
exampleSpecs.audience: a triage team of four people, fifteen minutes into an ambiguous presentation with competing explanations
exampleSpecs.stakes: the 30-minute window in which a different treatment path could change the outcome
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the attending has named a preliminary diagnosis and the team's language has shifted to organizing around it; the junior nurse catches a detail in the medication history that suggests a different cause — she hesitates because the attending has been right every time this month; the required beat is her deciding to voice it anyway, and the team reversing course on the preliminary path
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a curtained bay with a medication blister pack on the tray that the attending has not picked up
mustInclude: the attending's preliminary diagnosis already shaping team language
her hesitation and the social cost of voicing it
mustAvoid: clinical medicine detail that overwhelms the dissent beat
any domain overlap with earlier medical examples

exampleSpecs.domain: architecture firm design review where the structural engineer disagrees with the team's preferred building envelope
exampleSpecs.audience: a design team of six with a senior partner whose direction has shaped the last two weeks of work
exampleSpecs.stakes: a planning submission due in five days and a structural concern that could require significant redesign
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the structural engineer has been holding back a concern about the façade's load path because the partner is personally attached to the design; at the penultimate review, she names it — 'I need to flag something I should have said last week' — the team pauses a design the partner loved, adds two days to the schedule, and avoids a costly planning revision
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a design review table covered in printed plans and model sections, the team's energy already pointed toward submission
mustInclude: the explicit naming of the concern she had been holding
the schedule impact and the avoided worse outcome
mustAvoid: architecture or structural engineering technical content

exampleSpecs.domain: mountain rescue coordination team debating a route decision with a dissenting team member
exampleSpecs.audience: a rescue team of five, two hours into a search, with one member who doubts the team lead's route choice
exampleSpecs.stakes: reaching the missing hiker before weather closes in; the wrong route wastes 90 minutes
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: one team member has a different read on the terrain from her local knowledge — she has not voiced it because the team lead has more formal training and the group is moving — she speaks up at the trail fork; the team runs a 90-second discussion, switches routes, and finds the hiker 40 minutes later on the route she advocated
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a trail fork at treeline with fog rolling in, the team already moving in the default direction
mustInclude: the member's local knowledge vs. the lead's formal training
the outcome on the switched route

exampleSpecs.domain: pharmaceutical company's drug safety committee considering whether to extend a trial monitoring period
exampleSpecs.audience: a committee of seven safety scientists reviewing adverse event signals from a Phase III trial
exampleSpecs.stakes: extending the monitoring adds $3M in cost; not extending risks missing a delayed signal
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the committee chair has stated her view (the current monitoring period is sufficient) before the open discussion — the framing effect means four members have already adjusted their internal estimates toward her position; one member explicitly disagrees and provides a quantified rationale; the committee runs a structured anonymous estimate round before the final discussion, which reveals that three of the four apparent supporters had private reservations they had not voiced
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a committee room where the chair's opening statement is being written in the minutes before members have spoken
mustInclude: the three suppressed reservations revealed by the round

exampleSpecs.domain: navy submarine crew during a tactical exercise where a sonar technician hesitates to report an anomalous contact
exampleSpecs.audience: a crew of eight on watch, with an exercise score that rewards confident decision-making
exampleSpecs.stakes: the exercise scenario outcome and the real-life habit being drilled
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the sonar tech has a contact that does not fit the expected exercise pattern — she is unsure whether to report it or classify it as noise; the exercise culture has historically rewarded quick confident calls; she reports it anyway as 'possible contact, requires confirmation' — the watch officer investigates and finds it is relevant to the scenario; the exercise debrief credits the report as the critical decision
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a sonar display with an anomalous trace that does not match the expected exercise signature
mustInclude: the exercise culture pressure toward confident quick calls
the debrief credit for the hedged report

exampleSpecs.domain: jury deliberation room where one holdout asks an uncomfortable factual question that the other eleven had moved past
exampleSpecs.audience: eleven jurors who have formed a consensus and a twelfth who has a specific question about the timeline evidence
exampleSpecs.stakes: a verdict that will stand unchallenged if the twelfth does not voice the concern
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the eleven have been discussing punishment and sentencing implications for forty minutes — effectively post-verdict — when the twelfth juror asks about a fifteen-minute gap in the timeline that no one had addressed; the room goes quiet; the foreperson requests to see the exhibit again; the gap turns out to be significant; the deliberation restarts from the finding of guilt rather than from sentencing
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a jury room with verdict forms already pulled from an envelope, the foreperson's pen hovering over the first signature line
mustInclude: the eleven already in post-verdict mode
the restart of deliberation from the finding
mustAvoid: legal procedure detail beyond what the scene requires
any specific crime type that could distract from the team dynamics lesson

skillTargets: identify when groupthink is operating — the signals that dissent has become socially expensive
apply the aggregation principle — why the group estimate should be formed before individual views influence each other
analyze what structural conditions make psychological safety operational rather than just declared
distinguish collective forecasting from committee consensus — what is preserved in the former that is lost in the latter
evaluate when a team's agreement is genuine convergence vs. conformity pressure

tryThisNowSpec: Before your next team discussion on a forecast or decision, run a one-minute silent estimate round: each person writes a number before anyone speaks. Collect them before opening discussion. Note whether the range is wider or narrower than you expected. If the range collapses to near-consensus after you speak first, your opening framing was already shaping the group's estimates — that is groupthink beginning, not wisdom emerging.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one analytical passage explaining why dissent feels like disloyalty in real teams — the social cost is genuine, not imagined — and why the structural intervention matters more than asking people to be braver
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
